explanations: luna: The commentary hears nafs as a sip and water as what sustains it; in this scene water springs from the rock and each group knows its own drinking place. The verse adds a communal arrangement of access to the life-sustaining drink. | terra: Twelve springs burst from the stone and every group knows its own مَشْرَب; the command to eat and drink from God's provision makes an ordered water-share a divine gift and duty.

luna: The source section distinguishes its root ل ه م, an inward casting, from ordinary outward speech; 2:97 describes Gabriel bringing revelation to the Prophet’s heart by Allah’s permission. The verse gives a parallel of divine communication reaching the inner person, though its Qur’anic revelation is not the same claim as the section’s ilham. | terra: Gabriel brings revelation down upon the Prophet's heart by God's permission, a direct Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's description of a God-given thing entering inward awareness.

luna: The section’s ل ه م dictionary example is a young creature taking all it needs from its mother’s udder; 2:233 describes mothers nursing children for up to two complete years and assigns their provision to the father. It gives a human parallel in which nourishment and its allotted support are explicit. | terra: Mothers are to suckle children for two complete years, with support apportioned by recognized fairness; nursing, full completion, and measured responsibility all sharpen the source's suckling image.
terra: The river tests Saul's troops by a precisely limited drink—abstention except for one hand-scoop—showing water consumption itself becoming a measured moral trial.

luna: The source section pictures the self receiving its moral qualities and Thamud receiving a share for their wrong; 2:286 says a soul has what it earns and bears what it acquires. This links inner moral capacity with personal accountability. | terra: Each نَفْس receives the credit of what it earns and bears the liability of what it earns, a balanced formulation of the soul's individualized moral portion.
terra: Like Pharaoh's people and those before them, rejecters are seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ; the same phrase as 91:14 ties communal destruction to sins as the share that occasions it.
terra: Every soul finds both the good and the evil it did brought before it, joining the two moral poles to the individual soul and its received consequence.
terra: God says He will cast terror into the hearts of disbelievers because of their associationism, another specific negative content placed inwardly by divine action.
terra: Every نَفْس tastes death and receives its reward in full, joining the soul's tasting with the exact completion of what is due.
terra: Those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly are said to eat fire into their bellies, turning seizure of another's share into inwardly consumed punishment.

luna: The source section says Allah inspires the self with both fujur and taqwa; 4:79 says good is from Allah while evil is from the self. This is a specific theological boundary on how the two inner orientations are attributed, illuminating the difference between receiving a capacity and owning one’s deed.
terra: The believers are told to cooperate in righteousness and taqwa but not in sin and aggression, an enacted social separation of the two moral directions disclosed within the soul.

luna: The source section’s root ل ه م describes Allah placing something in the inner self; here Allah says He inspired the disciples to believe in Him and His messenger. This gives the inner reception a specific moral content, faith, alongside the section’s fujur and taqwa. | terra: God says He inspired the disciples to believe in Him and His messenger; divine inward prompting, its moral content, and رَسُول meet explicitly.
terra: Earlier, materially stronger generations are destroyed بِذُنُوبِهِمْ and replaced, another direct use of sins as the cause of a fully delivered communal consequence.
terra: God opens the chest of the one He wills to guide and constricts the chest of the one He wills to leave astray; opposed inward conditions make the moral alternatives bodily perceptible.

terra: The command to give full measure and weight with justice is paired with the rule that no soul is burdened beyond capacity; fair shares, exact measure, and the individual soul converge explicitly.
terra: A bad deed is repaid only with its like while a good deed is multiplied, making exact equivalence a boundary on the punitive share.

luna: Salih identifies the she-camel as a sign, tells his people to let her graze on Allah’s land, and forbids harming her. This spells out the warning carried by the section’s elliptical “camel of Allah and her drinking.” | terra: Salih names نَاقَةُ ٱللَّهِ as a sign, tells Thamud to let her eat on God's earth, and explicitly says not to touch her with harm; this is the expanded warning compressed into 91:13's camel and watering-right formula.
terra: The arrogant chiefs ask the believers whether they know Salih is sent by his Lord, keeping the messenger's authority under explicit debate between the camel warning and its violation.
terra: The arrogant reply that they disbelieve in Salih's message, supplying the inward stance that immediately issues in hamstringing the camel.

luna: The people hamstring the camel, reject Salih’s command, and challenge him to bring the punishment. This is a close parallel to 91:14’s denial and killing; the next verse gives the destruction. | terra: Thamud hamstring the she-camel, defy their Lord's command, and challenge Salih to bring the threatened punishment, connecting violation of the protected share to the people's demand for their own consequence.

luna: The earthquake seizes the people after they hamstring the camel in 7:77, leaving them fallen in their homes. It completes the same warning, violation, and destruction sequence as 91:13 and 91:14. | terra: The earthquake seizes the people after the hamstringing, supplying the punishment side of the section's exchange between the camel's denied portion and their resulting portion.
terra: Shuayb orders his people to give full measure and weight and not diminish what belongs to others, a direct ethical parallel to honoring another recipient's allotted share.

terra: Had the towns believed and practiced taqwa, blessings from sky and earth would have opened; denial instead brings seizure, linking moral response to whether provision or punishment is received.
terra: God says He could strike later inheritors of the land بِذُنُوبِهِمْ, extending the sin-consequence formula as a live boundary rather than only a past event.

luna: This parallel account says twelve springs burst forth and each group knew its drinking place. The source section’s image of the camel’s assigned water share is set beside an orderly distribution that gives every group a known place. | terra: The twelve tribes and twelve springs repeat the same scene: every people knows its drinking place, so communal difference is sustained by a divinely organized water allocation.

luna: The section pictures ilham as something Allah places within the self; this verse says Allah will cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. The inward placement recurs with an opposite content and audience, distinguishing moral orientation from fear imposed in battle. | terra: God inspires the angels and then says He will cast terror into disbelievers' hearts; this is the source dictionary's God-originating inward “casting” pattern filled with punitive fear rather than moral discernment.
terra: Pharaoh's house and earlier peoples are seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ after rejecting God's signs, repeating the exact causal vocabulary of the section's punishment-share.
terra: The same comparison culminates in “We destroyed them for their sins” and Pharaoh's people are drowned, pairing the root ذ ن ب with a water-borne destruction.
terra: People acknowledge their sins after mixing a righteous deed with another evil deed; both opposed moral contents are present in one human case, closely paralleling the soul's fujur and taqwa.
terra: When revelation descends, it increases believers in faith and they rejoice, showing divine speech entering recipients and augmenting one moral orientation.

terra: The same descending revelation adds impurity to those whose hearts are diseased, contrasting with its increase of faith in 9:124 and showing one divine input received according to opposed inward states.

luna: This is Salih’s warning about Allah’s she-camel: leave her to graze on Allah’s land and do not touch her with harm. It makes explicit the protective force of the short command “نَاقَةَ ٱللَّهِ وَسُقْيَٰهَا” in the source section. | terra: Salih again identifies God's she-camel as a sign, grants her access to God's earth, and warns his people not to harm her, making the protected animal and its divinely assigned use explicit.

luna: The people hamstring the camel, and Salih tells them they have only three days before the promised punishment. This is the direct counterpart to 91:14’s hamstringing and destruction; 11:64 supplies the preceding warning about the camel. | terra: After hamstringing the camel, the people receive a precisely bounded three-day respite, so even the interval before their promised consequence is measured out.
terra: When the command comes, God saves Salih and the believers by mercy while disgrace takes the violators, separating the shares of the messenger's two audiences.

luna: After the camel is hamstrung in 11:65, a blast seizes the wrongdoers. The verse gives the immediate destruction corresponding to the Lord’s action in 91:14; 11:68 states the lasting desolation. | terra: The blast seizes the wrongdoers after they violate the camel warning, repeating the immediate passage from denied animal right to received punishment.

luna: This continues the destruction in 11:67 by saying they were as though they had never lived there. It makes the totalizing force of 91:14’s “فَسَوَّىٰهَا” concrete in the parallel Thamud account.
terra: Shuayb again commands full measure and just weight and forbids depriving people of their things, restating the structure violated when a group preserves its access while denying the camel's.
terra: The water-drawer lowers his دَلْو into the well; it supplies the Quran's concrete bucket scene behind the source dictionary's definition of ذَنُوب as a water-filled bucket.

luna: The source section uses ن ف س for the self and says it receives both fujur and taqwa; 12:53 describes the nafs as urging evil, with an exception for those shown mercy by their Lord. It specifies the evilward tendency while bounding it by divine mercy. | terra: The speaker says the نَفْس persistently commands evil except where the Lord grants mercy, locating fujur-like pressure within the soul while preserving God's decisive gift.

terra: Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure, each carrying what fits it; measured reception by distinct vessels is a close natural parallel to souls and communities receiving apportioned contents.
terra: A tyrant is given festering water to drink in Hell; the act of being given drink remains, but divine سُقيا has become an allotted punishment rather than sustaining provision.

terra: He tries to gulp that drink yet can scarcely swallow it, while death comes from every side without ending him; failed ingestion reverses the effortless “one-mouthful” swallowing in the source dictionary.
terra: God holds the treasuries of everything and sends each thing down only in a known measure, supplying the hidden reserve and exact allotment that the section hears in an assigned drink.

luna: The source section identifies س ق ي as giving someone what they drink; 15:22 says “فَأَسْقَيْنَاكُمُوهُ,” presenting rainwater as something given to drink. It clarifies the provision side of the camel’s allotted drink. | terra: God sends water and فَأَسْقَيْنَاكُمُوهُ, while humans do not hold its stores; the same س ق ي family presents drinking as something God makes available from a reserve He controls.

luna: The source section’s root س ق ي concerns giving someone drink, and its camel is allowed to graze; 16:10 brings together water for people to drink and pasture for animals. It joins the same two necessities that surround the camel’s protected share. | terra: God sends sky-water from which people drink and vegetation grows for grazing, uniting the animal's drink, its pasture, and divine provision.

luna: The source section’s dictionary branch رَسْل links رسول with abundant milk; 16:66 describes pure milk from livestock as a drink. This supplies a concrete animal-milk scene for that secondary association, though the ayah itself does not use the root ر س ل. | terra: God gives drink from cattle's bellies as pure milk pleasant to drinkers; it realizes both the source's suckling image and its secondary رَسْل sense of abundant flowing milk.

luna: The source section labels ل ه م as its root for ilham and pictures a thing cast inward and swallowed; 16:68 says “أَوْحَىٰ رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ,” giving a concrete divine instruction received by an animal. The next ayah completes this bee scene with its drink. | terra: The Lord inspires the bee to establish its dwellings; this nonhuman instance broadens the section's God-originating ilham before the next ayah turns its result into a drink.

luna: This continues the inspired-bee scene of 16:68; its own contribution is that a drink comes from the bees’ bellies and is healing for people. It makes the section’s meeting of inward reception, animal life, and drink concrete in one passage. | terra: After the bee receives divine inspiration, a healing drink of varied colors emerges from its belly; inward divine direction and a drink held within a creature form a single sequence.
terra: Every soul comes pleading for itself and is paid in full for what it did, making full individual receipt the endpoint of moral action.

luna: The section’s paired fujur and taqwa lead into the people’s chosen wrong against the camel; 17:7 states that doing good benefits the self and doing evil is against it. It makes the consequence of moral direction return to the person who takes it.
terra: The command to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance repeats the requirement that apportioned rights be honored accurately.

luna: The source section presents the she-camel as Allah’s protected sign and recounts that Thamud killed her; 17:59 likewise names the she-camel of Thamud as a visible sign and says they wronged her. It makes the camel’s sign-status explicit while connecting mistreatment of her with rejection of a sign. | terra: God says He gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign and they wronged her; the whole water-right episode is named as a divinely supplied sign met by injustice.
terra: Those who appeal for relief are supplied water like molten metal that burns faces; the giver-and-drinker structure survives as a dreadful inversion of merciful provision.
terra: A garden's water may sink so deep that its owner cannot seek it, another concrete limit on the human assumption that an available water-share remains under personal control.

luna: The section joins divine inward instruction to maternal nourishment; 20:38 says Allah inspired Moses’ mother. The next verse, 20:39, supplies the content of that inspiration, while this ayah’s own contribution is to identify the mother as its recipient. | terra: God recalls inspiring Moses' mother with what was inspired, confirming that a divine communication can enter a non-prophetic human recipient before 20:39 unfolds its acts of casting.

luna: The section describes ilham as something cast into the inner person; 20:39 tells Moses’ mother to place him in a chest and the river, then says Allah cast love upon him. This gives the casting image a concrete infant scene; 20:38 identifies the command as inspiration to his mother. | terra: Moses is to be cast into the chest and river, while God says He cast love upon him from Himself; physical casting and a God-given inward quality overlap with the dictionary image behind ilham.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ن ف س says water is called nafs because the soul depends on it; 21:30 says every living thing was made from water. This makes the commentary’s water-as-condition-of-life association concrete beyond thirst. | terra: God makes every living thing from water, closely matching the source dictionary's claim that water can be called nafs because the living self subsists by it.
terra: Every نَفْس tastes death and is tested with both evil and good; tasting and the paired test make the soul itself an ingesting subject for contrary allotments.
terra: At the Hour every nursing mother is distracted from the child she suckles, a vivid boundary case in which the source's primal ingestion scene is violently interrupted.
terra: Those given knowledge recognize the revelation as truth, believe in it, and have their hearts submit humbly, a specific sequence from divine communication to inward reception.

luna: The source section develops drinking as a measured share; 23:18 says water is sent down “بِقَدَرٍ” and can be taken away. This makes explicit both the measure of water provision and its boundary. | terra: Water descends “in measure,” is lodged within the earth, and can be taken away, concretely joining a measured share, a hidden store, and the giver's continuing control.

luna: The section’s root س ق ي describes giving someone drink, and its dictionary note on ر س ل evokes successive milk; 23:21 says God gives people drink from livestock’s bellies. Alongside the camel’s assigned water share, this adds the complementary scene of an animal supplying drink to people. | terra: Livestock are a lesson because God gives people drink from what is within their bellies and also grants other benefits and food, directly extending the udder-and-ingestion scene.
terra: God creates every moving creature from water, applying the life-from-water claim specifically to animals and thus to the embodied creature at the water-share scene.
terra: God sends winds before mercy and pure water from the sky; this ayah supplies the source and purity of the water used to revive land and water creatures in 25:49.

luna: The section’s ن ف س dictionary note ties the soul’s standing to water; 25:49 describes rain reviving dead land and giving drink to many animals and people. It places the camel’s ration within water as shared provision for living creatures. | terra: Rain revives dead land and God gives it as drink to livestock and many people, placing herd and human drinking under one act of divine provision.
terra: God creates the human from water and establishes bonds of lineage and marriage, another precise Quranic basis for water as constitutive of the living self.
terra: Abraham identifies God as the One who feeds him and gives him drink, stating the giver-recipient relation that the section unfolds through سُقيا.

terra: Salih declares himself a trustworthy رَسُول in the same speech that reaches the camel's drinking share, keeping the messenger-word—and its milk resonance in the source dictionary—inside its original scene.

terra: Within Salih's address, Thamud are reminded that they dwell among gardens and springs; the disputed camel-turn therefore belongs to an explicitly water-rich setting whose abundance still has a binding order.

luna: The people tell Salih that he is bewitched, a specific refusal of the messenger whom 91:14 says they denied. The next verse demands a sign, and 26:155, 26:156, and 26:157 give the camel’s water share and their attack on her.

luna: Thamud demand a sign from Salih if he is truthful; this leads directly to the camel’s specified drinking turn in 26:155. It connects rejection of the messenger to the protected sign at the center of the source image.

luna: The section says the camel’s suqyā is a protected drinking share; Salih specifies that she has a turn to drink and the people have a known day’s turn. This is the clearest statement of the divided water right that the section reads in “وَسُقْيَٰهَا.” | terra: Salih assigns the she-camel one drinking turn and the people a known day's turn, the clearest parallel to the section's claim that سُقيا is a protected, apportioned right.

luna: After 26:155 assigns the camel and people their drinking turns, Salih forbids them to harm her and warns of punishment. This verse shows the boundary protecting the share described in the preceding ayah. | terra: The next instruction, not to touch the she-camel with harm, spells out the warning carried by the accusatives in 91:13 and ties violation of her water-share to the threatened punishment.

luna: The people hamstring the camel after Salih’s warning about her drinking in 26:155 and 26:156. This is the same violation and action named in 91:14; 26:158 gives the resulting punishment. | terra: They hamstring the she-camel and then become regretful, the decisive act that converts a divided water arrangement into culpability.

luna: Punishment overtakes the people after they hamstring the camel in 26:157. The verse supplies the consequence corresponding to “فَدَمْدَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ” in 91:14. | terra: The punishment takes them immediately after the hamstringing, completing the same action-and-recompense sequence condensed in 91:13–14.
terra: The command to give full measure and not be among those who cause loss directly opposes taking one's own complete portion while diminishing another's.
terra: The next command requires weighing with a straight balance, adding impartial measurement to the passage's demand for full shares.
terra: The people are forbidden to diminish others' things, completing the passage's concrete parallel to violating a divinely assigned entitlement.
terra: The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down; this ayah supplies the divine messenger of the descent whose destination is identified as the heart in 26:194.
terra: Revelation comes عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ so that the Prophet may warn; the heart is explicitly the receiving vessel for what descends from God.
terra: God sends Salih to Thamud to worship Him, but the people split into contending factions; it identifies the same messenger and the divided moral audience addressed by the camel warning.

terra: Salih asks his people why they seek to hasten evil before good and urges them to seek forgiveness; it matches their challenge to bring punishment after violating the camel warning and names the two outcomes they choose between.
terra: God directs attention to the outcome of the plot against Salih: He destroys the plotters and all their people, repeating the communal consequence attached to rejection of this messenger.
terra: God saves those who believed and practiced taqwa from that destruction, preserving the taqwa-side of the moral division within the Salih narrative.

luna: The section’s root ل ه م frames inspiration as something placed within; here Allah inspires Moses’ mother to nurse him and then cast him into the river. The verse joins inward divine instruction to the section’s concrete image of a young creature taking nourishment from its mother. | terra: God's inward communication to Moses' mother immediately commands her to suckle him; divine inspiration and a young one's taking milk meet in one ayah, just as the section explains inward inspiration through nursing.

terra: Moses' mother's heart becomes empty and God strengthens it so that she remains among the believers; this is a concrete divine intervention in the same inward recipient who was inspired to nurse him.

luna: The source section’s dictionary example is an unweaned young animal taking milk from its mother; 28:12 says Moses had been refused wet nurses before his own mother was brought to nurse him. This continues 28:7’s command to nurse him and completes the parallel feeding scene. | terra: God had prevented Moses from accepting other nursing women, making his reception of milk selective and preparing the restoration of the inspired mother-child bond.
terra: God returns Moses to his mother so that she may be comforted and know His promise is true; the nursing episode becomes the embodied fulfillment of the inspiration she received.
terra: Moses reaches a water source where shepherds are watering their flocks while two women hold theirs back, staging access to a shared animal-watering place and its social ordering.
terra: Moses waters the women's flock for them—فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا—an exact concrete instance of س ق ي as giving another creature what it drinks.
terra: God says each destroyed people was seized بِذَنۢبِهِۦ and then names their differing destructions, directly presenting sin as the individualized cause and measure of the share received.
terra: Every نَفْس tastes death and then returns to God, preserving the repeated Quranic pairing of the soul with an act of tasting.

luna: The source section describes the self as formed and receiving both moral directions; 30:30 describes people as created upon Allah’s fitrah. This offers a boundary on the moral image: a created disposition toward God is set beside the section’s account of both fujur and taqwa.
terra: Human progeny is made from an extract of humble fluid, preparing the fashioned, inwardly equipped human of 32:9 and reinforcing the living self's dependence on water-like substance.
terra: God proportions the human, breathes into him of His spirit, and makes hearing, sight, and hearts, showing a fashioned being equipped with the inward faculty that can receive.
terra: God casts terror into the hearts of the hostile People of the Book, repeating inward casting as an instrument of judgment.
terra: Livestock provide benefits and drinks, reinforcing the section's movement between the camel, the udder, and what creatures make available to drink.

terra: Mockers ask for their قِطّ, their portion, to be hastened before the Day of Account, resembling Thamud's demand that the threatened consequence be brought and the section's image of one's due share.
terra: God tells Job to strike the ground and identifies the resulting water as a cool washing place and drink, a personally assigned drink brought forth by direct divine provision.
terra: God sends water down, conducts it into springs within the earth, and brings out varied crops; this directly joins supplied water, hidden storage, and controlled release.
terra: God opens a person's chest to submission and gives light from Him, while hardened hearts stand in manifest error; opposed inward capacities clarify how divine guidance can be received.
terra: God's message makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to His remembrance, giving bodily form to revelation entering and transforming its recipients.
terra: Every soul is paid in full for what it did, a direct nonlexical parallel to receiving one's complete allotted share.
terra: Powerful former peoples are seized بِذُنُوبِهِمْ with no protector from God, making their worldly strength unable to alter their assigned consequence.

terra: God guided Thamud, but they preferred blindness to guidance and were seized by a humiliating blast for what they earned; moral disclosure, chosen fujur, and the people's earned consequence meet in one retelling.
terra: God saves those who believed and practiced taqwa from Thamud's blast, marking the boundary between the two moral receptions and their different shares of the outcome.
terra: God sends provision down in the quantity He wills lest abundance produce transgression, directly joining measured allotment with the recipient's moral response.
terra: The ayah marks revelation as one of the delimited ways God communicates with a human, clarifying the source claim that this kind of inward giving is from God's side.
terra: God reveals a spirit from His command to the Prophet, who had not known scripture or faith, and makes it a guiding light; this precisely depicts God-given inward disclosure producing guidance.
terra: God sends sky-water بِقَدَرٍ and revives dead land, presenting water itself as a measured allotment whose quantity and life-giving effect belong to Him.
terra: God says He apportions people's livelihood in worldly life, a direct statement that sustaining shares are divided by Him rather than seized on human terms.
terra: Creation culminates in every soul being repaid for what it earned without injustice, tying measured consequence to the soul that receives it.

luna: The source section labels ر س ل as the root of رسول and cites the secondary dictionary form رَسْل for abundant, successive milk; 47:15 pictures rivers of milk in Paradise. This is a specific milk-flow echo through the source’s dictionary branch, though the ayah itself uses لبن and does not call a messenger milk. | terra: Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste does not change, expanding the source dictionary's secondary image of رَسْل as copious, continuous milk.
terra: Those who accept guidance receive increased guidance and are given تَقْوَاهُمْ; this directly parallels the soul's receiving its taqwa from God in 91:8.

terra: God makes faith beloved and beautiful in believers' hearts while making disbelief, فسوق, and disobedience hateful, an explicit inward presentation of opposed moral possibilities akin to the soul taking in fujur and taqwa.
terra: The Thamud episode is invoked shortly before 51:59, locating that later “share like their companions'” within the fate of the very people who violated the camel's share.
terra: Thamud rebel against their Lord's command and the blast takes them while they look on; this is the particular predecessor whose fate helps define the “share like their companions'” in 51:59.
terra: After the blast, Thamud can neither rise nor defend themselves; this completes the predecessor-fate to which 51:59's allotted portion points back.

terra: God asks no provision from creatures and does not ask them to feed Him; before He names Himself the Provider, the giver-recipient relation is decisively reversed away from God as a needy consumer.
terra: Immediately before the wrongdoers' portion, God names Himself the Provider and possessor of firm power, setting sustaining provision and punitive allotment under one giver.

luna: The source section explicitly labels ذ ن ب as the root and reads ذَنُوب as a full bucket and a share; 51:59 uses “ذَنُوبًا” for the wrongdoers’ share like that of earlier peoples. Its own wording turns sin into an allotted portion; the preceding 51:43, 51:44, and 51:45 names Thamud and their destruction, connecting that comparison to the people in 91. | terra: ذَنُوبًا gives wrongdoers a portion like the portions of their predecessors; it is the Quranic use behind the source dictionary's “bucket/share” sense and turns punishment into the exact share awaiting them.
terra: Immediately after wrongdoers are assigned their portion, woe is pronounced for them on their promised day; this identifies the temporal destination of the share in 51:59.
terra: A human has only what he strives for, defining the personal basis of the share whose full recompense appears two ayat later.
terra: Human striving will be repaid with the fullest recompense, echoing the section's stress on a portion delivered without remainder.

luna: The source section says Thamud denied the messenger before hamstringing the camel; 54:23 states that Thamud denied the warnings. This verse supplies the rejection that leads into the camel trial in 54:27 and the water division in 54:28.

luna: Here Thamud object that they should follow one human among themselves, a concrete form of rejecting Salih as messenger. It sharpens the denial summarized in 91:14; 54:27, 54:28, and 54:29 then show the camel, her share, and the violation. | terra: Thamud object to following a single human from among themselves; it identifies their stance toward the messenger whose reminder they call “cast upon him” in 54:25 and whose camel follows.

luna: Thamud ask whether the reminder was sent to him alone and call him a liar. This specifies what their denial of the messenger entails in the source section; 54:27, 54:28, and 54:29 continue with the camel and her drinking share. | terra: Thamud mockingly asks whether the reminder was “cast” upon one man among them; أَأُلْقِىَ ٱلذِّكْرُ closely stages the source dictionary's image of something cast inward, inside the very passage that proceeds to the camel and her water.

luna: This verse warns that the people will learn who the liar is, immediately before the camel is sent as a trial in 54:27. It connects the source section’s denial and punishment to the trial that follows.

luna: Here the she-camel is sent as a trial for Thamud, and they are told to watch and wait. The next verse, 54:28, specifies the divided water share central to the source image. | terra: God says He is sending the she-camel as a trial and commands watchful patience; the sent animal, the messenger-root resonance, and the test of honoring her assigned share converge here.

luna: The source section’s root س ق ي includes setting drink aside for someone to take; here the water is explicitly “قِسْمَةٌۢ بَيْنَهُمْ,” with each drinking turn attended. It turns the camel’s protected share into an explicit allocation. | terra: God orders Salih to announce that the water is divided between camel and people and that every drinking turn is attended, directly joining provision, partition, and enforceable entitlement.

luna: The people call their companion, who takes up the task and hamstrings the camel. This supplies the agent and act compressed into 91:14; the preceding 54:28 has assigned the water share they violate. | terra: Thamud call their companion, who takes action and hamstrings the sent she-camel; this is the concrete breach of the water test announced in 54:27–28.

luna: This ayah points readers to the terrible punishment and warnings after the camel is hamstrung in 54:29; 54:31 supplies what happened, one blast and dry stalks. Its own contribution is the warning that follows the act, echoing the consequence named in 91:14 and the lack of fear in 91:15. | terra: God asks how His punishment and warnings were, marking the consequence as the answer to the camel test and its rejected warning.

luna: After 54:30’s warning about punishment, this verse says Allah sent a single blast and the people became like dry stalks. It gives the specific aftermath to the destruction compressed in 91:14. | terra: A single blast leaves them like crushed pen-stalks, giving the physical result of violating the apportioned water arrangement.
terra: Everything is created according to measure, giving the broad divine principle behind a fashioned soul, a timed water turn, and a commensurate consequence.
terra: People must establish weight with justice and not make the balance deficient, a general boundary against reducing another's measured due.
terra: The people of the left must drink boiling water after eating from the tree of zaqqum, turning ingestion into the medium of their consequence.
terra: They drink like desperately thirsty camels, a stark reversal of the protected she-camel whose lawful drinking turn must not be violated.
terra: The listener is asked to consider the water being drunk, fixing attention on the very act and object treated as an assigned gift in the section.
terra: The question whether humans sent the water down from the cloud or God did identifies the true provider of the drink considered in 56:68.
terra: God could make drinking water bitter; the threatened transformation marks the limit between an available, palatable share and a drink that cannot sustain.
terra: Believers are asked whether the time has come for their hearts to humble to God's remembrance and revealed truth, presenting the heart's proper reception of what descends from Him.
terra: God places compassion and mercy in the hearts of Jesus' followers, furnishing another positive inward quality that comes by His act.
terra: God writes faith in the believers' hearts and supports them with a spirit from Him, a durable inward inscription of moral orientation from the divine source.
terra: God casts terror into the exiles' hearts so that they demolish their own houses, showing an inwardly received state producing outward consequence.
terra: Whoever believes in God has his heart guided by God, a concise statement of divine action within the moral recipient.
terra: If divorced mothers suckle the children, fathers must give them their due payment and consult fairly; nursing is again sustained by an apportioned human obligation.
terra: If people's water sinks beyond reach, the ayah asks who can bring flowing water; it exposes the boundary of human control over the drink God assigns and stores.
terra: Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming calamity, another concise retelling of the particular people's received consequence after the camel episode.
terra: Had people remained straight on the way, God says He would have given them abundant water to drink; water provision is explicitly linked to moral stance.
terra: The abundant water of the previous ayah is itself a test, clarifying that a generous drink-share, like the camel's, can expose obedience rather than merely satisfy need.
terra: Every نَفْس is held in pledge for what it earns, joining the soul as recipient with the individualized moral share produced by its acts.
terra: The oath by the self-reproaching نَفْس presents the soul as an inward moral witness, complementing 91:8's disclosure of fujur and taqwa within it.
terra: The human was a drop of emitted fluid before being created and proportioned in 75:38, supplying the liquid origin immediately before the act of making fit.
terra: From a clot, God creates and proportionates the human—فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ—another direct instance of the fashioning that precedes the soul's moral reception in 91:7–8.

luna: The source section says the self receives both fujur and taqwa; 76:3 says the human is shown the way and may be grateful or ungrateful. The verse makes the inner moral alternatives legible as contrasting responses. | terra: God guides the human to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful; the two possible responses parallel the opposed moral contents disclosed to the soul.
terra: The righteous drink from a cup blended with camphor, presenting an assigned drink as the concrete form of their moral outcome.
terra: God's servants drink from a spring that they cause to gush abundantly, closely matching the source dictionary's sense of a drink made available for its recipient to take freely.
terra: Their Lord gives the blessed a purifying drink—وَسَقَىٰهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ—an explicit positive instance of God Himself assigning what is drunk.
terra: God sets firm mountains and gives people sweet water to drink, another direct use of س ق ي for an inhabitable world's allotted provision.
terra: The transgressors find neither coolness nor drink in Hell, first presenting deprivation of the very sustaining share the section makes visible.
terra: Their only drink is boiling water and pus, converting a denied refreshment into a punitive portion.
terra: That drink is called a fitting recompense, making the preceding punitive portion exactly correspond to deeds as the section's “full bucket-share” does.

luna: Salih’s camel is permitted to graze on Allah’s land and has a protected water turn; 79:31 pairs the earth’s water with its pasture. The verse brings together the two resources that the camel scene allocates and protects. | terra: God brings the earth's water and pasture out of it, pairing the two necessities granted to grazing animals in the camel scene.

luna: This verse calls the water and pasture in the preceding creation sequence provision for people and their livestock. It makes the camel’s grazing and drinking share part of the wider provision given to humans and animals. | terra: The water and pasture brought out in 79:31 are identified as provision for people and their livestock, completing the shared sustenance scene.
terra: The one who fears standing before the Lord restrains the نَفْس from desire, showing the enacted taqwa-side of the soul's two inward possibilities.
terra: God pours water down abundantly, beginning a sequence that ends by naming the resulting growth as provision for humans and livestock.
terra: God splits the earth open after pouring the water, showing the drink-bearing provision entering and opening its receiving ground before growth appears.
terra: Fruit and pasture are among what the watered, split earth produces, adding the grazing side of the camel's drink-and-pasture scene.
terra: The entire water-and-growth sequence is called provision for people and their livestock, uniting both classes of recipients under one divine supply.
terra: The human addressee is reminded that God created, proportioned, and balanced him; سَوَّاكَ makes the soul's fitness in 91:7 part of a repeated creation pattern.

terra: Those who take a measure from others يَسْتَوْفُونَ—take it in full—echo the source dictionary's form استوفاه for the young animal exhausting the udder and expose the injustice of securing one's whole share.
terra: The same people diminish what they measure out to others, a precise ethical reversal of taking one's own full portion while obstructing the camel's allotted portion.
terra: God creates and proportionates—خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ—closely repeating 91:7's making the soul fit before its inward moral endowment.
terra: God measures and then guides—قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ—placing exact determination beside guidance as 91:7–8 place fashioning beside inspiration.
terra: The humbled faces are given drink from a boiling spring—تُسْقَىٰ—using the same giving-to-drink relation for punishment rather than care.

luna: The section’s fujur and taqwa name two moral directions received by the self; 90:10 says God showed the human being the two ways. This gives the paired inner orientations an image of alternatives made visible. | terra: God says He showed the human the two high roads, a compact nonlexical parallel to making both fujur and taqwa perceptible.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good sees it, making even the smallest positive moral portion perceptible and fully returned.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil sees it, completing the exact two-sided measure of moral consequence.
